extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers interested in Johnny Carson, television history, and late-night comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style biographical article summarizing Johnny Carson's career, influences, personal life, legacy, and impact on late-night comedy and popular culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of success on The Tonight Show
rubrics_metrics.description: For a comedian appearing on the show, getting Carson to laugh and being invited to the guest chair were considered the highest honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Getting Carson to laugh and earning an invitation to sit in the guest chair functioned as de facto markers of a performer's success and acceptance on the program. Implicit anti-pattern: performing material that doesn't earn Carson's reaction or recognition (no laugh, no guest-chair invite) indicated a weaker appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid politicizing the show / keep the program non-political
rubrics_metrics.description: He also seldom invited political figures onto the Tonight Show because he 'didn't want it to become a political forum' and did not want the show used ... to influence the opinions of the viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a hosting principle, the show avoided turning into a vehicle for political debate or persuasion. Carson stated he 'hates to be pinned down' and avoided expressing political views on air; hosts/productions following this model should minimize overt political content and invitations that might steer audience opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect personal privacy and limit personal disclosures on air
rubrics_metrics.description: He normally refused to discuss politics, social controversies, his childhood, and his private life with interviewers, and offered a list of pre-written answers to inquiring journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carson maintained a clear boundary between on-camera persona and private life: avoid detailed personal revelations in interviews, prepare canned/plain replies for intrusive questions (examples cited: 'Yes, I did,' 'Not a bit of truth in that rumor,' 'No, kumquats'). Anti-pattern: extensive public airing of private matters that could undermine an entertainer's public role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine personal experience for comedic material (with discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the divorce, Carson frequently used its financial terms as a source of comedic material on the Tonight Show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal experiences (including painful or embarrassing ones) can be repurposed as material — e.g., Carson turned elements of his divorce settlement into jokes. Guidance implied by the page: such material can be effective but is used selectively and as part of a crafted on-air persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer mentorship and joke-sharing among late-night comedians
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to his death, Carson occasionally sent jokes to David Letterman; Letterman used these jokes in the monologue of his show, and in his first broadcast after Carson's death Letterman delivered a monologue compiled entirely of jokes sent in by Carson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal mentorship and sharing of material between established and successor hosts/comedians is a recognized practice; contributing jokes to peers can shape a successor's monologue and reflect professional camaraderie. Example: Carson supplying material to Letterman, who publicly acknowledged it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety/vaudeville-style format and showcasing diverse talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Carson was the successor to The Ed Sullivan Show as a showcase for different types of talent, as well as continuing a vaudeville-style variety show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful late-night/show format, per Carson's example, includes booking a range of performers (comedians, musicians, novelty acts) and functioning as a career-launching platform. Implicit expectation for hosts: curate diverse acts and provide opportunities that can elevate performers' careers.
